intro: If you earn money on the side — Etsy, Uber, freelance gigs, consulting, OnlyFans, Airbnb — the IRS treats you as a sole proprietor and you owe **self-employment (SE) tax of 15.3%** on net earnings above $400, layered on top of regular federal income tax and any state income tax. SE tax is the self-employed version of FICA: 12.4% Social Security (capped at the $176,100 wage base for 2026) plus 2.9% Medicare (uncapped, with an extra 0.9% Additional Medicare on earnings above $200k single / $250k MFJ). Because no employer is withholding for you, the **CPA rule of thumb is to set aside 25–30% of every gross dollar** for federal income tax + SE tax + state, and to send four **quarterly estimated payments via Form 1040-ES** (due April 15, June 16, September 15, and January 15 of the following year for the 2026 tax year). Miss those deadlines and the IRS charges an underpayment penalty currently running ~8% annualized. The good news: every legitimate **Schedule C business deduction** (home office, mileage, supplies, software, health insurance) reduces both income tax *and* SE tax base, and side-hustlers can shelter big chunks of net SE earnings inside a **Solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA** — up to a combined $72,000 for 2026 ($70,000 in 2025). This calculator quantifies your real after-tax take-home, the SE tax bite, your quarterly payment, and the QBI 20% deduction under §199A so you can plan the year instead of getting surprised in April.
keyTakeaway: A side hustle earning $30,000 net in the 22% bracket typically owes ~$4,239 SE tax + ~$4,559 federal income tax = ~$8,798 total, keeping roughly $21,202 — about 70.7 cents on the dollar.

explanation:
## How self-employment tax actually stacks on top of income tax

When a W-2 employee earns a dollar, the employer withholds 7.65% FICA (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare) and matches another 7.65% silently. A self-employed side-hustler owes **both halves** — that's the 15.3% SE tax. It is layered on top of federal income tax (and any state income tax), so the marginal hit on the next dollar of side-gig profit is materially higher than the same dollar of W-2 wages.

## The SE tax math, worked out on $30,000 net side-hustle profit

- SE tax base = $30,000 × 0.9235 = **$27,705** (the 0.9235 multiplier mirrors the employer-side FICA deduction W-2 employees enjoy automatically)
- SE tax = $27,705 × 0.153 = **$4,239.87** → rounded for planning at **$4,240**
- Half of SE tax = $2,120 is an **above-the-line deduction** on Schedule 1, line 15, reducing AGI
- Federal income tax in the 22% bracket on ($30,000 − $2,120) = $27,880 × 0.22 ≈ **$6,134** before QBI
- §199A QBI deduction (20% of QBI, simplified, assuming under phase-out) ≈ $5,576 → fed income tax drops to roughly **$4,907**
- All-in federal hit ≈ $4,240 SE + $4,907 income tax = **$9,147**, an effective federal rate of ~30.5% on the $30k of net profit. Add state and the total commonly lands at **33–36%** — which is why the planning rule of **set aside 25–30% of gross** (not net) keeps you out of trouble.

## Schedule C deductions every CPA reaches for

Every dollar deducted on **Schedule C** lowers SE tax base, federal income tax base, and (usually) state income tax base — a triple-stack win:

- **Home office**: simplified method = $5/sqft up to 300 sqft / $1,500 cap; actual method = pro-rated mortgage interest, utilities, insurance, depreciation. Requires regular and exclusive business use (IRS Pub 587).
- **Business mileage**: **67¢/mile for 2024**, IRS sets each year; or actual vehicle expenses pro-rated by business use percentage. Mileage log required (date, miles, purpose).
- **Section 179 / bonus depreciation**: equipment, computers, furniture deductible immediately up to **$1.16M Section 179 limit (2024)**. Most side-hustlers fully expense in year one.
- **Software, phone, internet, subscriptions**: deductible pro-rated by business use. Adobe, Canva, ChatGPT Plus, QuickBooks, Zoom — all fair game.
- **Meals**: **50% deductible** when business-related (client meetings, travel). The 100% restaurant meal deduction expired after 2022.
- **Self-employed health insurance**: 100% above-the-line deduction (Schedule 1) for premiums paid for you, spouse, dependents — limited to net SE income.
- **Retirement contributions**: Solo 401(k) and SEP-IRA contributions are above-the-line, deductible against SE income (but **not** against SE *tax* base — they reduce income tax only).

## QBI §199A — the 20% deduction that quietly saves thousands

The Qualified Business Income deduction lets eligible pass-through owners (sole props, S-corps, partnerships) deduct **up to 20% of qualified business income** before federal income tax. **2026 phase-out begins at $241,950 single / $483,900 MFJ** (inflation-adjusted from $191,950 / $383,900 for 2024). Below the threshold, almost any side-hustle gets the full 20%. Above it, **Specified Service Trades or Businesses (SSTBs)** — consulting, health, law, accounting, financial services, performing arts, athletics — phase out fast and lose it entirely once fully phased. Non-SSTB businesses (e-commerce, Etsy, freelance writing, software dev, real-estate flippers) keep QBI subject to W-2 wage and qualified property tests at higher income.

## Solo 401(k) vs. SEP-IRA vs. SIMPLE IRA — the tax shelter decision

For 2026 the **combined contribution limit (employee + employer) is $72,000** in 2026 ($70,000 in 2025) plus $8,000 catch-up at age 50+:

- **Solo 401(k)**: employee elective deferral up to **$24,500 in 2026** (IRS Notice 2025-67, up from $23,500 in 2025) + employer profit-sharing up to 25% of net SE earnings. Best for maxing out at modest income levels because the employee portion is a fixed dollar amount, not a percentage. Roth option available.
- **SEP-IRA**: employer-only contribution up to 25% of net SE earnings, simpler paperwork, no annual Form 5500. Better for high-net-profit single-owner shops that want minimal admin.
- **SIMPLE IRA**: $16,500 (2025) employee limit, cheap setup, no Form 5500. Mostly used when there are employees.

Contributions reduce federal income tax base but **not** SE tax base — the IRS taxes the gross net SE earnings before retirement contributions for SS/Medicare purposes.

## Quarterly estimated payments — Form 1040-ES

The IRS requires estimated payments if you expect to owe at least **$1,000 in federal tax** after withholding. The four 2026 deadlines: **April 15, June 16, September 15, and January 15, 2027**. The safe-harbor rule: pay the lesser of (a) 90% of current-year tax or (b) 100% of prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI > $150k). Underpayment penalty rate is currently ~8% annualized. Most state DORs run a parallel quarterly schedule.

## State-level wrinkles

States with no income tax (AK, FL, NV, SD, TN, TX, WA, WY) keep things simple. NH taxes only interest/dividends. California self-employed can voluntarily opt into SDI; New York PFL is generally voluntary for self-employed. Most graduated-bracket states (CA, NY, OR, MN, NJ) tax SE income at the same rates as wages, but treatment of QBI varies — some states fully decouple from §199A.

faq.q: How much should I set aside for taxes from my side hustle?
faq.a: For most side-hustlers in the 22–24% federal bracket, set aside **25–30% of every gross dollar** received (before expenses). That covers SE tax (~15.3% of net), federal income tax (10–24% marginal), and a typical state tax (3–7%). Higher earners over $250k AGI should bump to 35–40% to absorb the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax and possible loss of QBI. The cleanest discipline: open a separate high-yield savings account, sweep 30% of every payout into it immediately, pay 1040-ES from there quarterly.

faq.q: Am I required to make quarterly estimated tax payments on 1099 income?
faq.a: Yes if you expect to owe at least **$1,000 in federal tax** after any W-2 withholding and credits. Form 1040-ES vouchers are due **April 15, June 16, September 15, and January 15, 2027** for the 2026 tax year. The safe harbor: pay the lesser of 90% of current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI > $150k). Miss it and the IRS applies an underpayment penalty — currently ~8% annualized — calculated on Form 2210.

faq.q: Solo 401(k) vs SEP-IRA — which is better for a side hustle?
faq.a: **Solo 401(k)** wins for most one-person businesses because the employee elective deferral ($24,500 in 2026, up from $23,500 in 2025) is a fixed dollar amount on top of the 25%-of-net-SE employer profit-sharing — meaning you can max out tax-deferred contributions much faster at modest income. **SEP-IRA** wins only if you want zero admin: employer-only contribution capped at 25% of net SE earnings, no Form 5500, no plan document. Both share the **2026 combined limit of $72,000** (up from $70,000 in 2025). Solo 401(k) also allows Roth contributions and loans; SEP-IRA does not. Both reduce income tax base but not SE tax base.

faq.q: Home office deduction — simplified or actual expense method?
faq.a: **Simplified method**: $5 per square foot up to 300 sqft, hard cap **$1,500**. Zero recordkeeping beyond proving the space exists and is used regularly and exclusively for business. **Actual expense method**: pro-rate mortgage interest (or rent), utilities, insurance, depreciation, repairs by the business-use percentage (business sqft ÷ total home sqft). Usually beats simplified once your home office is 200+ sqft and total home costs are above ~$25k/year — but you must add back depreciation as ordinary income when you sell the home. Either way, IRS Pub 587 requires **regular and exclusive** business use of an identifiable space.

faq.q: What is the 2026 standard mileage rate for business use of a vehicle?
faq.a: The IRS sets the standard mileage rate annually. For 2025 it is **67¢ per business mile** (up from 67¢ for 2024); the 2026 rate is typically published in December and historically moves a few cents. Track every business trip with date, miles, and purpose — apps like MileIQ, Stride, or Everlance handle this. Alternatively use the **actual expense method**: pro-rate gas, insurance, maintenance, depreciation, lease payments by business-use percentage. You cannot switch from actual back to standard mileage on a vehicle you previously depreciated using actual expenses.

faq.q: Do I qualify for the §199A 20% QBI deduction?
faq.a: Almost certainly yes if your **2026 taxable income is below $241,950 (single) / $483,900 (MFJ)** — the full 20% deduction is available regardless of business type. Above those thresholds, **Specified Service Trades or Businesses (SSTBs)** — consulting, health, law, accounting, financial services, performing arts, athletics — phase out and lose QBI entirely once fully phased ($291,950 single / $583,900 MFJ approximately). Non-SSTBs (e-commerce, freelance writing, software, real estate development) keep QBI subject to W-2 wage and qualified property tests. QBI is calculated on **Form 8995** (simple) or **Form 8995-A** (above phase-out).

faq.q: Hobby vs. business — how does the IRS decide and why does it matter?
faq.a: If the IRS reclassifies your side hustle as a hobby, you cannot deduct expenses against the income (post-2018 TCJA killed miscellaneous hobby deductions), so you pay tax on gross — brutal. The IRS uses a **9-factor test** (Treas. Reg. §1.183-2) examining whether you run it businesslike, depend on the income, have expertise, change methods to improve profitability, and so on. The **presumption rule**: profit in **3 of the last 5 years** is presumed a business (2 of 7 for horse breeding). Keep a separate business bank account, written business plan, profit-improvement notes, and a logo/website — these are cheap and bulletproof against hobby reclassification.

faq.q: Should I elect S-Corporation status to reduce SE tax?
faq.a: Worth modeling once net SE profit exceeds **roughly $50,000/year**. An S-Corp pays you a **reasonable W-2 salary** (subject to FICA) and lets you take the remainder as a **distribution** — distributions are not subject to SE tax. Example: $100k net profit as a sole prop = ~$14,130 SE tax; same $100k as S-Corp with $60k reasonable salary = ~$9,180 payroll tax, saving ~$4,950/year. Offsets: payroll service ($600–$1,200/year), S-Corp tax return ($800–$2,000), state franchise fees (CA $800/year minimum, NY ~$25–$4,500 graduated). File **Form 2553** within 75 days of formation or by March 15 for current-year election.

faq.q: What happens if I have a W-2 job and a side hustle at the same time?
faq.a: SE tax is calculated only on your self-employment net profit. But your W-2 Social Security wages count toward the **$176,100 (2026) SS wage base**. If your W-2 already exceeds $176,100, the 12.4% SS portion of SE tax on your side income is **zero** — only the 2.9% Medicare portion applies (plus 0.9% Additional Medicare if combined income exceeds $200k single / $250k MFJ). You can also bump W-2 withholding via a new Form W-4 to cover the side-hustle income, avoiding 1040-ES quarterlies entirely — withholding is treated as evenly distributed across the year and bypasses underpayment penalty math.

faq.q: Is Airbnb / short-term rental income subject to SE tax?
faq.a: Usually **yes** if average guest stay is **less than 7 days**, or less than 30 days when you provide substantial services (cleaning between stays, meals, concierge). Report on **Schedule C**, owe SE tax 15.3%. Long-term residential rentals (30+ day stays, no substantial services) go on **Schedule E** as passive rental income, **exempt from SE tax**. The distinction comes from Treas. Reg. §1.1402(a)-4 and is a frequent IRS audit issue for Airbnb hosts. Real estate professional status (750+ hours, more than half of personal services) can also allow loss deduction against W-2 income, but the bar is high.

faq.q: What state tax rate do I enter if I live in a no-income-tax state?
faq.a: Enter **0**. No personal income tax states for 2026: **Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, Wyoming**. New Hampshire taxes only interest and dividends as of 2025 (the I&D tax fully phases out in 2027). If your state uses graduated brackets (CA, NY, OR, MN, NJ), enter your **effective marginal rate** at your expected total taxable income for the most accurate estimate. Note: many states do not conform to the federal §199A QBI deduction — verify on your state DOR website.
